06a3bee7-1756-596e-90e4-49becb64c66e.name: Royal Brigantine
06a3bee7-1756-596e-90e4-49becb64c66e.description:
Responsible for the construction and design, Torquato José Clavina was the foreman ship's carpenter at the Naval Arsenal, much admired for his skill and competence. The brigantine is a magnificent work in gilded wood, crafted by the artist Manuel Vieira, while on the broadside is a panel of zoomorphic elements over darkened gold. In the Queen Maria I style, the barge is painstakingly decorated with pinnacles, friezes, caryatides, flower-like ornaments and tile panels depicting vases of flowers in frames. On the posterior panel of the quarterdeck cabin, there is a painting of Pedro Alexandrino de Carvalho, who was responsible for painting the sovereign's private cabin. The quarterdeck cabin stands out from all the others for its richness and beauty, notably for the framed Venetian mirrors. The lower poop panel has complex and beautiful ornamentation: Amphitrite and Neptune are represented in two bas-reliefs surrounded by gilded-wood floral borders.  
On board were 78 paddlers with 40 oars, which made the barge glide through the water with the help of the boss and the bow oarsman. Throughout its history, the barge transported several monarchs and heads of state.  
With the first French invasion of November of 1807, the barge was assigned to take Queen Maria I and the rest of the royal family to the *Príncipe Real*, the ship on which they would escape to Brazil. Likewise, it was from this galley that King João VI disembarked in Lisbon following this turbulent period.  
Later, on his first State visit in 1903, King Edward VII of England chose his oldest ally: Portugal. The Royal Brigantine headed for the British ship HMS *Victoria and Albert* to receive the monarch. This visit was followed by series of other State visits, amongst which were the visits of Kaiser William II of Germany, Émille Loubet, President of the Republic of France, and King Albert I of Belgium. The brigantine was always present.  
During the Republic, the brigantine was neglected and did not glide over the river for 40 years. In 1957, on the occasion of the official visit of Her Majesty Queen Elizabeth II, the barge crossed the waters of the Tagus for the last time.  
In 1963 it became part of the collection of the Museu de Marinha (Naval Museum) where it underwent restoration. The quality of the restoration saw the museum receive several honourable distinctions including that given by the World Ship Trust.
06a3bee7-1756-596e-90e4-49becb64c66e.short_description:
In 1780 Queen Maria I ordered the construction of a grand royal barge: the Royal Brigantine of Queen Maria I. Its construction was destined to celebrate the betrothal of Prince João (future King João VI) to the Spanish Princess Carlota Joaquina, in 1784.  
Symbol of power and a jewel of naval archeology, the brigantine represents more than 200 years of historical pageantry.

The bridge made it possible for the Orient Express to reach Constanţa, a Black Sea port, from where ships went to Istanbul, whereas in the past the journey implied people being ferried on the Danube from Romania to Bulgaria, travelling by train to Varna (a Bulgarian Black Sea port) and then taking a ship to Istanbul. The “Carol I” bridge, which was designed by engineer Anghel Saligny and was at that time the longest in Europe, was inaugurated on 29 September 1895. In his inaugural speech, the king declared that “Romania is now owner of the shortest route between the northern seas and the countries of the Orient”.

1027a1b3-31c5-5bc1-9a9d-4a4a487bcc6d.name: Char-de-côté diligence
1027a1b3-31c5-5bc1-9a9d-4a4a487bcc6d.description: The British publisher John Murray travelled through the canton of Jura by stagecoach in 1838. He later described the trip in his *Hand-Book for Travellers* as “very rough” – hardly surprising, since the travelogue author was riding in a char-de-côté. On this type of coach, which was used primarily in France and western Switzerland, the carriage body was set at right angles to the undercarriage, so that the passengers sat sideways (*de côté*) in relation to the direction of travel. This was more uncomfortable, but it allowed these carriages to be built with a narrower wheelbase, and as a result the char-de-côté could be used even on those roads in the canton of Jura that were narrower than the standard track width of 1.4 metres. Today, no travel writer would have cause to complain about the quality of Swiss public transport, which is one of the best in Europe.

148b5238-d0f6-5a73-ade6-65b1ffbc8ca4.name: Palanquin
148b5238-d0f6-5a73-ade6-65b1ffbc8ca4.short_description:
The palanquin from India, a symbol of royal power, is comprised of a wooden compartment with a woven floor and roof resembling an arch or two oyster halves seated on large poles. Engraved decorations, various shapes and motifs enhance the carriage. Thin drapes protect from prying eyes and cover the fortune carried inside the carriage. Only men of certain castes or elephants were allowed to bear the palanquin transporting royals on long journeys and brides to their wedding ceremony.  
  
Across the Arabian Peninsula, palanquins receive the name *howdah* (*hawdaj*,) and carried Bedouin women on a camel’s back, frequently appearing in the poetry of the Murrah tribe. Since 1266, another variation called *mahmal* ceremonially transferred the cover of the Kaaba with the Egyptian pilgrimage to Mecca. Today, palanquins might be represented as the predecessors of bullet-proof cars with tinted windows, escorting royals and their entourage.

1e164505-7b44-5ab0-8ab5-124407905064.name: Model of the brig *Mariţa*
1e164505-7b44-5ab0-8ab5-124407905064.short_description: In 1834 Wallachia and Moldavia, which were under Ottoman suzerainty, were granted by the Ottoman Empire the right to sail on the Danube using their national banners. The first Romanian ship to sail under Romanian banner was the brig “Marița”, built in the naval dockyard of the Giurgiu port. Its owner was Wallachian politician Alexandru Vilara, who gave it the name of the wife of Alexandru II Ghica, Wallachia’s ruler between 1834-1842. “Marița” began its first trip in December 1834. Its destination was Istanbul, where it transported 300 kg of wheat. It returned in June 1835 after having been seriously damaged by two storms, one of which on its way back, when the crew had to throw overboard the wine purchased from Istanbul.

All these features were originally influenced by the design of Portuguese ships.

2735c542-1b56-59a7-9fac-72518fe82535.short_description:
In 1900 the Ottoman Sultan Abdülhamid II (r.1876–1909) began the construction of a railway line connecting Damascus to the holy cities of Medina and Mecca. Built by public subscription and with an appeal to Muslims of the world for financial support, the railway line began from Damascus and reached Medina in 1908, never reaching Mecca.  
This map, which is dated 28 Huzayran 1334 (28 June 1916), shows the Hijaz railway line from Damascus to Medina and Dar‘a to Haifa, with a dotted line marking the line between Medina and Mecca (a line which was never completed). Names of stops and tribal territories are marked. The map is signed by the German Heinrich August Meissner – the chief engineer of the Hijaz railway. In 1904 he was given an official title and was known as Meissner Pasha. The original sketches for Hijaz railway maps were made by Mukhtar Bey, an accomplished engineer from Istanbul who was responsible for the original surveys of the route. They were then drawn by other officers and the blue prints signed off by Meissner, perhaps with changes. Mukhtar Bey was known as ‘Meissner’s right hand man’. The date here is notable as the Arab Revolt, which saw sections of the railway destroyed, began in June 1916.

30d81d9b-e0ff-5637-818a-498c9971880e.name: Coach belonging to King João V
30d81d9b-e0ff-5637-818a-498c9971880e.description:
A brilliant example of a royal ceremonial vehicle, the coach was built in Portugal during the first half of the 18th century. It is generally agreed that it was commissioned by King D. João V for his personal use. Its gilt carving is attributed to the sculptor José de Almeida whose brother, Felix Vicente de Almeida, was an architect and sculptor attached to the royal household. The coach clearly reflects the transition between the Louis XIV and Louis XV styles, although there is also an obvious Italian influence in the decoration. This is not surprising since José de Almeida studied in Rome under Carlo Monaldi. According to Max Terrier the coachwork may have been executed by Filipe Juvara, an Italian sculptor working in Portugal for King D. João V.  
The main features are the elegant curving lines and the Rococo-style rippling movement enhanced by the *bombé* shape of the side panels and doors, typical of Regency furniture during the period (1715–1723). The four side-sections of the body bear elegant carvings of female figures holding castles, attended by genii. The bodywork is covered by woodcarving and chiselled bronze finials, handles and springs, in the form of young women's heads, known as *espagnolettes*, much in vogue all over Europe at the time. According to Luciano Freire the paintings were executed by José da Costa Negreiros, a Portuguese painter and a disciple of André Gonçalves. On the other hand Luis Keil believes the painting could be attributed to the French painter, Pierre Antoine Quillard, (1701-33) a disciple of Antoine Watteau. Apparently, Quillard arrived in Lisbon to serve the Portuguese court where “he executed not only religious paintings but also portraits, palace interiors and coach panels”.  
The interior of the coach is lined with rich red velvet and the rear wheels are decorated with small carvings representing the 12 signs of the zodiac.

3198ae9c-013b-5b14-b430-71d27c928c5a.name: Sedan chair
3198ae9c-013b-5b14-b430-71d27c928c5a.description: The sedan chair is a typical shape, with an S-curve back, a door at the front and a graceful roof. The slender gilt structural framework, which is curved and mobile, has moderate carved volutes and leaf and shell motifs. The door and sides are equipped with glazed apertures, which open by lowering. The remaining surfaces are light green with the edges painted with a dignified garland of multicoloured flowers. Painted on the upper panel of the chair-back is the Dubrovnik-based patrician Zamagna family’s coat of arms. The graceful roof, covered with black leather, secures with a decorative edging of brass. There are two fitments for the shafts on the sides. The interior has one seat located at the rear. Like the cushion, the seat upholstery is red silk damask. The curtains are white silk damask enhanced with haberdashery trimmings.

341be9d6-6bac-5978-aa0e-844e03633f92.name: The port of Brăila
341be9d6-6bac-5978-aa0e-844e03633f92.short_description: In 1829, an annex to the peace treaty of Edirne, that was concluded after the Russo-Ottoman war of 1828-1829, concerned the Principalities of Wallachia and Moldavia. One of its provisions was that the Sublime Porte had to give back to Wallachia the three cities situated on the left bank of the Danube, which it had conquered in the 15h-16th centuries. Among these was Brăila, a port on the Danube annexed by the Ottomans at around 1540. After 1829 measures were taken by the local authorities for the modernization of Brăila. The port subsequently developed thanks to the growth of Wallachian commerce as a consequence of the fact that by the treaty of Edirne the Ottoman Empire granted the freedom of commerce to the Romanian Principalities. In 1838 Brăila was given the status of free port (with no or few customs duties).

372e3810-b18e-5d0c-b107-9bd837cefb1e.name: Hijaz Railway Medal
372e3810-b18e-5d0c-b107-9bd837cefb1e.description: Medal of the Hijaz Railway fund. In September 1900, (the 25th anniversary of Sultan Abdul Hamid’s accession to throne) he addressed a call for all the Muslims all over the world to collect donations for establishing a railway between Damascus and the holy places to facilitate transporting the pilgrims. The call was responded to enthusiastically and with great support from all Muslims. Sultan Abdul Hamid II began the donations with 300,000 Ottoman gold lira, then kings and heads of Islamic world donated money or materials for setting the railway. The donations continued till 1907. On this occasion the sultan issued gold, silver and nickel medals to donors – for instance a nickel medal given to whoever donated 5-50 Lira, a silver medal for whoever donated 50-100 Lira and named them bey, and for donations of more than 100 Lira a gold medal and the title of Pasha. After that the donation become compulsory in which the officials disclaim a one month salary. This is a gilt nickel medal issued AH 1318 / AD 1900. On its obverse, within a wreath: tuğra of sultan Abdul Hamid II with "al-Ghazi" and form of locomotive and the date ١٣١۸ (AH 1318) below. On reverse, حميديه حجاز تيمور يولنه خدمت ايدن حميتمندانه مخصوص مدالية در ("Medal reserved to patriots who have served the Hamidiye Hijaz Railway") written in Divan script.

3879757a-f06b-5c78-885b-5bf3ddf848b8.short_description: The Hijaz Railway was a narrow-gauge railway (1,050mm/​3ft, 5 11⁄32 in track gauge) that ran from Damascus to Medina, through the Hijaz region of Saudi Arabia, with a branch line to Haifa on the Mediterranean Sea. It was a part of the Ottoman railway network and was built to extend the line from the Haydarpaşa Terminal in Istanbul beyond Damascus to the holy city of Mecca. It got no further than Medina, 400 kilometres (250mi) short of Mecca, due to the construction interruption caused by the outbreak of World War I. The main purpose of the railway was to establish a connection between Constantinople, the capital of the Ottoman Empire and the seat of the Islamic Caliphate, and Hijaz in Arabia, the site of the holiest shrines of Islam and the holy city of Mecca, the destination of the Hajj (annual pilgrimage).

4543ccbf-dceb-5300-941b-8c2f10ba3b29.short_description: After the Russian annexation of Bessarabia (the eastern part of Moldavia) in 1812 and until the restoration by Russia of Southern Bessarabia (1856), Galați remained Moldavia’s only port on the Danube. Understanding the city’s importance for Moldavia’s economy and wanting to ensure its development, prince Mihail Sturdza, who was appointed ruler of Moldavia by the Sublime Porte in 1834, issued in 1836 an act stipulating that Galați was to be a free port (with no or few customs duties) starting with March 1837. Also, a new neighborhood was to be built based on modern urban planning prescriptions and Galați received the right to organize annually five national fairs, during which traders from everywhere could sell any type of products.

45d767b4-fcfa-5a22-97f1-6135821c6624.name: Figure sleigh 'Triton'
45d767b4-fcfa-5a22-97f1-6135821c6624.description: The “Triton” sleigh at the Swiss National Museum is one of the most interesting and beautiful pieces of the respective collection. Built in the second half of the seventeenth century, it belonged to the family Pfyffer von Altishofen. The sculptures’ exquisite carvings are attributed to the artist Hans Wilhelm Tüfel (1631–1695) of Sursee. The style elements such as the dolphins’ open mouths, the “Triton”, and the fish on the runners were inspired by the Fontana del Tritone at Piazza Barberini in Rome. The Pfyffer family had close ties to Rome, given that, over the course of time, eleven family members served as commanders of the Swiss Papal Guard. Special features of the sleigh include that it could be drawn by either one or two horses and that the large open shell provided space for two passengers apart from the driver who sat on a special platform at the back. Showpiece sleighs like this were used primarily by the nobility for their pleasure outings through the snowy winter landscape and during carnival. The sleigh was donated to the museum by a wealthy brewer from Zofingen in 1934 and now presents itself again in its original splendour.

4acd8717-82fe-538c-b4c9-53b16ce962bb.name: The plan of Haydarpaşa Train Station
4acd8717-82fe-538c-b4c9-53b16ce962bb.short_description: The original plan of Haydarpaşa Train Station, viewed from northern frontage. In 1871 Sultan Abdülaziz ordered a rail line to be built from Haydarpaşa to İzmit. Haydarpaşa station opened in 1872, and in 1888 the Anatolian Railway (CFOA) took over the line and the station. Since the station was built next to the Bosporus, freight trains would unload at Haydarpaşa and the freight would be transferred to ships. Haydarpaşa was chosen to be the northern terminus of the Baghdad Railway and the Hijaz Railway in 1904 and with rail traffic increasing, a new and larger building was required. The Anatolian Railway hired two German architects, Otto Ritter and Helmut Conu, to build the new building. They chose a neo-classical structure and construction started in 1906.

4b55c559-2654-5a6f-a502-72a32dfa2c6a.name: Photo of the Aswan Railways inauguration
4b55c559-2654-5a6f-a502-72a32dfa2c6a.short_description: The inauguration of the Aswan Train Station, with `Adli Yakan Pasha; Muhammad Najib al-Gharabli Pasha; Husayn Rushdi Pasha; Tharwat Pasha; Fathallah Barakat Pasha; Morkos Hanna Pasha; al-Dagwi Bek, director of Aswan; and Mahmud Shakir Bek, deputy undersecretary of the Ministry of Transportation in attendance. The Egyptian railway line was the first to be established in Africa and the Middle East, and the second worldwide after the United Kingdom. The establishment of the first railway line in Egypt began on 12 June 1851, and it became operable in 1854. The Egyptian railway construction project supervisor at that time was British engineer Robert Stephenson, son of the famous inventor of locomotives, George Stephenson. The Aswan train station is one of the most important railway lines constructed during the reign of King Fu`ad.

The messengers, who conveyed dispatches throughout the country, were identified as the Tatars. Private or personal correspondence was not a part of that relay system; it was built to fulfil governmental needs. Because of this reason the *reaya* (public) created an alternative postal method by using caravans, pilgrims, and private couriers called *ulaks*. The *Tanzimat* Decree, which was the declaration of process included reformation, modernization and westernization in 1839, proved that the Ottoman Empire was focused on its policy of changing governing to be more like modern Western European-style administrative practices.

Its ships were used as troop transports during the Crimean War, and were so helpful for the army that the Emperor gave the company the right to operate on the Bordeaux-Brazil route as thanks. This was the first French transatlantic line equipped with steamers. The following year, the *Société générale maritime* (later called *Compagnie générale transatlantique*) received the North Atlantic lines. From 1871 to 1914 the shipping company, now called *Compagnie des messageries maritimes*, saw its Golden Age.

61eb1293-6209-599c-bd83-34f180e3bec2.short_description: The Black Sea port of Constanța underwent its first modernization while Dobruja, the province where it is situated, was under Ottoman control. In 1857, when the Ottoman government hired a British company to build a railway in Dobruja, the concluded contract also stipulated the reconstruction of the Constanța port. Completed in 1864, it was still a small harbor with a wooden dock, a dam and one cereals depot. After Dobruja was annexed by Romania, a law was issued in 1885 for the “improvement and augmentation” of the port. In 1896 its modernization was leased to a French enterprise but due to some disagreements, three years later the state took over the works, which were led by architect Anghel Saligny. Inaugurated in 1909, the new port had 3 dams, several docks, depots, silos, an oil basin, an electric plant.

It connected with the first railway line at Riyaq. The connection between Aleppo and Beirut, a well-equipped and sizeable port, decreased trade in Alexandretta, the traditional port for merchandise leaving or entering Syria. Alexandretta was not connected to Aleppo by rail until 1914. Aleppo and Northern Syria became increasingly important as links between Damascus and Beirut were consolidated. This also marked the increasing importance of Beirut as a powerful city in the region and not only as a Mediterranean port.

The cost of the project was estimated at approximately five million Ottoman golden lira which were provided from: donations, the revenues of the Ottoman State earned from the sale of the stamps, and a special tax upon all the citizens for the railway. Construction of the narrow-gauge track (105cm) whose axle weight was (10.5 tonnes) began in 1900 with a wire telegraph line along its side connecting Damascus with Medina across Amman with a total track length of 1303km. The construction of the project ended in 1908. All the tracks and the stations were completed as detailed below: Mezerib Dera'a section, September 1901; Dera'a Al-Zarqa section, September 1902; Al-Zarqa Amman section, September 1903; Amman Ma'an section, September 1904; Ma'an Tabuk section, end of 1906; Tabuk Medain Saleh, September 1907; Medain Saleh Medina, September 1908. These rails were brought from the destroyed railroad tracks that were harmed by Arab revolt army attacks in 1917. On one side of the first rail is an Arabic phrase written in divan script: "*min khayrat mawlana Amir al-mu'minin al-sultan al-ghazi 'abdal-hamid khan thani 'azza nasruhu*".

713a80ee-86ad-5103-bcf7-5c70eb44eb3b.name: The interior of Tabuk Hospital
713a80ee-86ad-5103-bcf7-5c70eb44eb3b.short_description: In 1900 the Ottoman Sultan Abdülhamid II (r.1876–1909) began the construction of a railway line connecting Damascus to the holy cities of Medina and Mecca. Built by public subscription and with an appeal to Muslims of the world for financial support, the railway line reached Medina in 1908, but didn't reach Mecca. It was built with the assistance of German engineers who worked closely with Turkish officials. This album of the Hijaz Railway probably belonged to a Turkish engineer who worked on the construction of the line. It has 50 photographs, mostly of stations and sections of the line, but also of the landscape that the line passed through in the area between Tabuk and Mada’in Salih. The photographs were most likely taken by J. H. Halladjian, an Armenian photographer with a studio in Haifa in Palestine active in the 1890s and early 20th century. Based on records at the Imperial War Museum and The Royal Geographical Society, Halladjian took photographs of the Hijaz Railway and places along its route. The album contains some important photographs such as the one of the hospital at Tabuk which was established in 1907 and which became the railway’s quarantine station (ARC.al 6.16) as well as images which demonstrate the hardship of cutting through rock in order to pass the line through mountainous terrain (ARC.al 6.24). Also documented here are the great stone monoliths north of Mada'in Salih (ARC.al 6.38) in Mabrak al Naga, where prior to the Hijaz Railway, the Ottoman government connected the Hijaz to Istanbul via a telegraph line which reached Mada'in Salih in 1900. The building of the overland telegraph line between Damascus and Medina, much like the construction of the Hijaz Railway project to follow, was fraught with complications including the terrain and the danger of Bedouin resistance.

74dafe7a-b3e7-5be6-b35d-e97ef0242008.short_description:
In 1890, political pressure from Italian Prime Minister Francesco Crispi secured construction of the cruiser Bascir for the Moroccan Navy for the Fratelli Orlando shipyards located in Livorno (Italy), winning against French competitors.  
The Bascir was the first cruiser built by an Italian shipyard for a foreign navy after Italian unification in 1860. It was delivered to Morocco in 1894. Among its amenities was a hamam (in Western Europe often known as Turkish Bath), expressly requested by the buyer.

Seven years later in 1920 he visited Algiers for the first time, and went on to spent a few months there every year henceforth. He also lived in Algiers for the duration of the Second World War. Marquet was friendly with most of the artists from the Algerian school, and exhibited his paintings in galleries in the centre of town. Many of his paintings were on the theme of Algiers' harbour. His style, which was characterised by the luminosity and clarity he saw in North Africa, was an important early influence on the Algerian painter Mohamed Temam.

On its cover, the route runs from London and Paris to Marseille, divides as it crosses the Mediterranean and meets again in the Levant, before continuing to Baghdad and onwards to India, Southeast Asia and Hong Kong, a journey of eight days and more than 15,000 kilometres. A Dewoitine D-338 airliner, cut open to reveal its passengers, crew and cargo, promises comfort as well as speed. At the European end of the route stands a woman in an evening gown, while at the far eastern end another woman appears in East Asian dress. Inside, timetables, fares, visa regulations and currency tables guide the traveller across a map divided by colonial and mandate rule. Before the summer season was over, the outbreak of the Second World War disrupted this network of long-distance civilian air travel.

a3c1cda7-3cd5-5acd-9fe6-bbcc3a97be64.name: Photograph of Bab Idris street
a3c1cda7-3cd5-5acd-9fe6-bbcc3a97be64.description: Pictured here is Bab Idris street, leading to Bab Idris, the city's western gate and the entrance to the old town. By the time of Ahmad Bey al-Jazzar's reign (1777–1804), the city had four main gates: Bab al-Dirka to the south, Bab al-Santiya to the west, Bab al-Dabbagha to the north, and Bab al-Saraya to the east. Jazzar Pasha built fortifications between these four main gates, which was not a fortified gate. Other city gates included Bab Yaqub, also in the east, Bab Abu Nasr at Burj square, and Bab Idris. These non-military gates are reflections of the city's rapid expansion, particularly due to an increase in trade.

a6877d51-e0ec-5242-8b80-88d89c3d2ab4.name: Gare Chemin de fer Bagdad, Alep (Aleppo-Baghdad Railway Station)
a6877d51-e0ec-5242-8b80-88d89c3d2ab4.description: The postcard depicts Aleppo's Baghdad Railway Station, with the French description: Alep – Gare Chemin de fer Bagdad (Aleppo-Baghdad Railway Station), completed in 1912 as the northern Syrian terminus of the Baghdad Railway branch linking the city with Muslimiyeh station and the main line toward Mesopotamia. Situated in what became known as the Baghdad Station district, north of Aleppo's historic centre, the station was part of the development of a new modern quarter organised around transport and commerce. The station was constructed of stone masonry with broad overhanging roofs supported by timber brackets, pointed-arched openings and a monumental entrance pavilion. It was connected to the Baghdad Railway by a branch rather than the principal trunk line. The station became a strategic commercial gateway linking Aleppo with Anatolia in the north, and Mesopotamia as part of the wider Ottoman railway network.

b1ada77d-4a0f-5105-a292-423509ecec6b.name: Haydarpaşa Train Station
b1ada77d-4a0f-5105-a292-423509ecec6b.short_description: In 1871 Sultan Abdülaziz ordered a rail line to be built from Haydarpaşa to İzmit. Haydarpaşa station opened in 1872, and in 1888 the Anatolian Railway (CFOA) took over the line and the station. Since the station was built next to the Bosporus, freight trains would unload at Haydarpaşa and the freight would be transferred to ships. Haydarpaşa was chosen to be the northern terminus of the Baghdad Railway and the Hijaz Railway in 1904 and with rail traffic increasing, a new and larger building was required. The Anatolian Railway hired two German architects; Otto Ritter and Helmut Conu to build the new building. They chose a neo-classical structure and construction started in 1906.

The concession was later fortified when the company gained from the Customs the sole rights to store and carry all the transit goods passing through the Customs. Constructions works namely a maritime dam to expand and develop the Port were accomplished and the opening on the occasion of the accomplishment of these works was celebrated by the end of 1894, basins were developed and spread between Ras Al Shamiah and Ras Al Mudawar. It forms the midpoint of three continents: Europe, Asia and Africa, which makes the Port a passage for ship fleets between East and West. During the mid 70's, the Port of Beirut was an important international trading station with the surrounding Arab countries and up until today it has preserved its commercial nature.

The Manaki brothers shot their first film merely 10 years after the Lumiere brothers. In 1905, they shot their grandmother Despina spinning wool with women from the neighbourhood. Their first film of ethnographic value was shot soon after. It documents celebration of the feast of St. Cyril and Methodius in front of the Church in Bitola devoted to these saints. In their films, the Manaki brothers strived to document visually events from everyday life and to frame them as real works of art. In 1921, they projected the first film in the open-air arena at the Shirok Sokak Street in Bitola.

d51c4926-dec8-5d72-9ed4-34a107dddbd4.short_description: Istanbul’s geographic position between Europe and Asia and on the only sea route that connects the Black Sea with the Mediterranean gave Istanbul great strategic importance. The control of the Bosphorus, which connects the Black Sea with the Sea of Marmara, was repeatedly at stake in the 19th and early 20th centuries. This 1910 watercolour gives a wonderful impression of the bustling shipping and trading activities on the waters surrounding the city of Constantinople at the time. The view is taken from the Galata side of the city, looking across the Golden Horn towards its historic heart, dominated by imperial Suleymaniye mosque on the right and Bayezid tower in the centre. The Galata bridge, in its third incarnation as completed by the British firm G. Wells in 1875, can be seen connecting the two shores. Sailing boats like those seen here brought in wheat, spices and wood. The emergence of the steamship later in the century lead to enormous increase in the speed and volume of commodities shipped to Constantinople.

dc22fbbb-3a0b-58bb-82f9-7523c4e9d4d5.name: Official Hijaz Railway postcards
dc22fbbb-3a0b-58bb-82f9-7523c4e9d4d5.short_description: In 1900 the Ottoman Sultan Abdülhamid II (r.1876–1909) began the construction of a railway line connecting Damascus to the holy cities of Medina and Mecca. Built by public subscription and with an appeal to Muslims of the world for financial support, the railway line began from Damascus and reached Medina in 1908, never reaching Mecca. The financing for the Hijaz Railway was initially meant to come entirely from charitable donations and in May 1900 Sultan Abdülhamid II began the process with a sizeable donation from his personal funds. Despite national and foreign generosity towards the donations campaign, it soon became clear that this alone was insufficient to raise the funds needed for the construction. Therefore, the government sought to raise funds in many other ways, including the commission of postcards amongst other German-made products, in order to generate further yield. With the title ‘*Vue du chemin-de-fer Hamidié de Hedjaz*’ and with labels in French and Turkish, the postcards depict the construction of the Railway as well as general views and inauguration celebrations. These were available for purchase at local post offices.

ea3a91f8-4029-5f91-8e55-44b4089bf748.name: *Bayt al-Barudi steamship murals, Damascus*
ea3a91f8-4029-5f91-8e55-44b4089bf748.short_description: The steamships are of one of the most important technical innovations in the nineteenth-century, because they introduced new modern possibilities of transport and trade and hence contributed to the economic transformation of the Ottoman Empire. Because of this new transportation, cities on the Euphrates or Tigris experienced drastic changes and flourished even more. This impact lead to numerous depictions of steamships in artwork, such as this mural from Bayt al-Qabbani (Damascus, built at the turn of the 19th/20th century) shows. As symbols of the new time they represent global exchange of goods, ideas and people.

In Italy at the time, only the journal *Il Secolo* had a "Marinoni".

efe60dc6-7155-5eb3-a180-d0bfbd548106.name: Revenue stamp
efe60dc6-7155-5eb3-a180-d0bfbd548106.short_description: A revenue stamp issued in 1888 during the reign of Khedive Muhammad Tawfiq with the value of one dime. Written at the top is “Egypt Post” in Arabic with its French translation below it. To the left is the value of the dime in French, and in the centre is an image of one of the Giza pyramids and the Sphinx. The first postal stamp was issued in England in 1840. It bore the portrait of Queen Victoria, as suggested by Sir Roland Hill. This stamp was issued twice, in red and in blue. The United States of America was the second country in the world to use stamps, and the first Egyptian stamp was issued in 1866 by order of Khedive Ismail.

f542a798-8c47-5278-ad25-50059baf16a0.name: Distance marker (milestone).
f542a798-8c47-5278-ad25-50059baf16a0.description:
A distance marker or milestone usually erected to indicate distance between two stations along a pilgrimage or trade route, this one belonging to the period of the fifth Umayyad caliph, 'Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan (r. AH 66–86 / AD 685–705). The milestone is nearly square and has an inscription incised on its surface. The inscription consists of eight lines of *kufic* script. It cannot be read in its entirety because the upper section of the milestone has broken off and is missing. The legible portion reads: 'The slave of God, the commander of the faithful 'Abd al-Malik – may God's mercy be upon him – erected this stone. From here to Damascus is 109 miles'.  
  
Very few inscriptions have survived from the Umayyad period to the present. In addition, this milestone is significant because it shows the stylistic development of *kufic* script on stone during the Umayyad period.  
  
How was object obtained by museum: The inventory states that the object was transferred from the ruins of Khan al-Hatrura at Eriha (Jericho) to the Tiled Pavilion (Çinili Köşk) in 1884 as part of the 19th-century initiative to collect artworks from across the country. The object was transferred to the Museum in 1941.
f542a798-8c47-5278-ad25-50059baf16a0.short_description: In the early years of Islam, distance markers were erected on important trade and pilgrimage routes in order to show the distances to the travellers. These milestones bear date, patron names and toponyms related to the region, and are thus of documentary importance.
f542a798-8c47-5278-ad25-50059baf16a0.holder: Museum of Turkish and Islamic Arts.
f542a798-8c47-5278-ad25-50059baf16a0.dimensions: Height 40 cm, width 30 cm, depth 9 cm.
f542a798-8c47-5278-ad25-50059baf16a0.method_for_datation: The object was dated to 66–86 / 685–705 based on the mention in the inscription of 'Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan, who was the caliph during this period.
f542a798-8c47-5278-ad25-50059baf16a0.method_for_provenance: Inventory records indicate that the object was found amongst the ruins of Khan al-Hatrura at Eriha and taken to the Tiled Pavilion in 1884. Since Khan al-Hatrura is further from Damascus than the inscription would infer (109 miles) it is thought that the milestone was brought to the khan from a place further to the north.

The object was transferred to the Museum in 1941.

fe87deef-c455-5755-9f18-175550fef06e.name: Opening of the bridge over the Kishon (Qishon) River in the Jezreel Valley (?). A train festooned with Ottoman flags and carrying many pasengers is on the bridge, and dignitaries stand on the track.
fe87deef-c455-5755-9f18-175550fef06e.description: The photograph records an opening ceremony at a railway bridge, tentatively identified as a crossing of the Kishon River, also known as Nahr al-Muqatta‘, in the Jezreel Valley. A train decorated with Ottoman flags and carrying numerous passengers stands on the bridge, while dignitaries gather on the track. Conder and Kitchener described the Kishon as Palestine’s most important river after the Jordan, tracing a course of approximately 23 miles (37 km) from its spring-head west of Mount Tabor to the sea. Their survey records a width of approximately ten yards (9 m) and a depth of four feet (1.2 m) east of Tell el-Kassis in June 1875. Marshy ground and steep banks made crossings difficult along parts of its course, providing geographical context for the construction of railway bridges.

W., The Survey of the Western Palestine Memories Of The Topography, Orography, Hydrography, and Archaeology. Vol. (L), Sheets (VI) for The Committee Of The Palestine Exploration Fund, London (1881)
